summary: Describes how TCP/IP header fields behave, in the context of header compression. Many fields stay static or change predictably, so understanding their behavior in detail is key to designing a compression scheme. It plays a role like the analysis in RFC 3095 does for other headers. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Packet labels repeat a lot of the same information. This studies which parts stay the same and which change, so a shorthand can be made.

questions: what is tcp ip field behavior
how does header compression work for tcp
why is the tcp checksum not used for compression
subtitle: Which IP and TCP header fields stay put, which drift, and which are pure noise, for people designing header compression.

tldr.problem: To compress TCP/IP headers well, a designer needs to know exactly how each header field behaves from packet to packet, and TCP fields are much less predictable than RTP ones.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sorts every IPv4, IPv6 and TCP field into classes such as STATIC, INFERRED and CHANGING, studies which fields can be copied between flows, and describes the change pattern of each changing field and each TCP option.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational input to compression design, playing the role for TCP/IP that RFC 3095 plays for UDP and RTP. It does not define a compression scheme itself.

today: RFC 4413 is an Informational RFC from March 2006. Its metadata shows it is not obsoleted and not updated. It supplies analysis for compression design in the manner of RFC 3095 and does not itself define a compression scheme.

sections.title: Why Study Field Behavior
sections.content:
Header compression works because most header fields do not vary randomly from packet to packet. This memo describes how TCP/IP header fields behave within a TCP flow, following the method RFC 3095 used for UDP and RTP. The IP header is covered again because it behaves slightly differently from the RFC 3095 case.

The analysis has two steps: a general classification (Section 2) and a detailed look at change patterns (Section 4), with a study of how field values can be shared between flows (Section 3). The baseline is currently deployed TCP implementations that support IETF-standardized mechanisms.

One transparency point runs through the whole document: reserved bits cannot be assumed to be zero forever, so a compression scheme should cope with any use of them, even though it cannot optimize for uses not yet defined.
sections.eli5: If you mail the same kind of letter every day, the address barely changes. This document studies which parts of a packet are like that address, so they can be written down once.

sections.title: The Field Classes
sections.content:
Each header field gets one of five general classes. INFERRED fields can be derived from other values, such as the frame size. STATIC fields stay constant for the stream and need to be sent once. STATIC-DEF fields are static and also define the stream (addresses, ports, flow label). STATIC-KNOWN fields have well-known values and need not be sent. CHANGING fields vary.

For IP, the packet length and the IPv4 header checksum are INFERRED, the version, protocol and next header fields are STATIC, and the addresses are STATIC-DEF. The IPv4 reserved and Don't Fragment flags are treated as CHANGING so future uses are not blocked. In TCP, the ports are STATIC-DEF, the data offset is INFERRED, and everything else, including the sequence and acknowledgement numbers, flags, window, checksum, urgent pointer and options, is CHANGING.

The RFC totals the headers at 40 octets for IPv4 plus TCP and 60 octets for IPv6 plus TCP, excluding options.
sections.eli5: Some parts of a label can be worked out from the envelope, some never change, and some change every time. Sorting them into piles shows what is worth shrinking.

sections.title: Sharing Context Between Flows
sections.content:
When several flows to the same host happen at once or one after another, their headers look alike. The idea of replication is to start a new flow's compression context from an existing one, then overwrite whatever differs.

The RFC marks each field as replicable or not. Addresses, hop limit or TTL, window and the IPv4 identification context can be replicated. Sequence and acknowledgement numbers cannot, because Initial Sequence Number randomization (RFC 1948) makes them uncorrelated. Among TCP options, MSS, Window Scale and SACK-Permitted tend to have the same values across flows, so the compressor should keep them in the context even though they appear only in SYN segments.

Replication has a cost in complexity and robustness, and it needs the compressor to be confident the source data is present at the decompressor. The RFC suggests it helps most for series of short-lived connections, such as web browsing with HTTP/1.0.
sections.eli5: If you visit the same friend again and again, you already know their address. A new trip can start from the old one, and you only fix what changed.

sections.title: How the Changing Fields Behave
sections.content:
Changing fields are sorted into patterns: STATIC, SEMISTATIC (usually static, with brief changes that revert), RARELY-CHANGING, ALTERNATING between a few values, and IRREGULAR.

In IP, the DSCP is not expected to change often, though a route change could alter it. The two ECN bits are treated as the ECT and CE flags, and the RFC suggests assuming ECN with nonces as the baseline. The IPv4 Identification field depends on the sender's policy: sequential per stream is best, a shared counter gives sequential jumps, and a random policy forces two extra octets in every compressed header. The DF flag is expected to be stable when path MTU discovery is used, and TTL or hop limit is constant or alternates among a few values after route changes.

In TCP, the sequence number moves by the payload size (SYN and FIN each count as one) but can sit anywhere in the TCP window, so no one-size encoding fits. Acknowledgement numbers usually advance about twice as fast in bulk transfer, with one ACK for about every two full-size segments. The ACK flag is set on all but the first SYN, and PSH is effectively random. The checksum must be treated as random, and a scheme should add its own error detection. The Urgent Pointer must be carried so its value is preserved, since the checksum covers it.
sections.eli5: Some numbers on the label count up like a ticket machine, some flip between a couple of values, and some are random like dice. Each kind needs a different shorthand.

sections.title: TCP Options
sections.content:
Options sit at the end of the TCP header, are covered by the checksum, and the header is padded with zeros to a multiple of 32 bits. The RFC treats all options as changing and walks through each kind. Kinds 0 (End of Option List) and 1 (No-Operation) have no data, so a compressor only has to signal that they are present, and padding can simply be dropped.

MSS (kind 2) is only sent on SYN segments, and values such as 1460 for Ethernet and 536 as the default are common. Window Scale (kind 3) is a power of 2 between 0 and 14. SACK-Permitted (kind 4) has no data. SACK (kind 5) carries up to 4 blocks that can be viewed as offsets from the acknowledgement number. Echo and Echo Reply are obsoleted by Timestamps (kind 8), but a scheme should still be able to carry them as generic options.

Because the data offset field is 4 bits counting 32-bit words, the TCP header can be at most 60 bytes, which leaves 40 bytes for options. A compression scheme must support any option, including ones not yet defined.
sections.eli5: Options are extra sticky notes on the label. Most are stuck on only the first packet, and the rest of the time a short note saying that a sticky note exists is enough.

sections.title: Other Observations and Security
sections.content:
The RFC adds several design notes. A TCP bulk transfer spends less than 3% of a 1460-octet packet on header, but a pure acknowledgement is all overhead, so optimizing the ACK direction pays off. TCP fields change more independently and unpredictably than RTP fields, which makes a good efficiency and robustness trade-off harder. TCP has no obvious master sequence number, so one may need to be added explicitly.

On security, the RFC says it raises no direct concerns because it only describes field behavior. Where IPsec AH is used, compression must be transparent, and where IPsec ESP is used the TCP fields may be hidden, which prevents compression.
sections.eli5: Shrinking a label that rides on a big package saves little, but shrinking one on an empty envelope saves a lot. Locked envelopes cannot be shrunk because nobody can see inside.

viz.caption: OVERALL FIELD SIZES BY CLASS, IP PLUS TCP

items.title: STATIC
items.text: Classified as changing in general, but static under extra assumptions.

items.title: SEMISTATIC
items.text: Usually static; occasionally changes, then reverts after a known number of packets.

items.title: RARELY-CHANGING
items.text: Changes occasionally and then keeps the new value.

items.title: ALTERNATING
items.text: Switches between a small number of values.

items.title: IRREGULAR
items.text: No useful change pattern can be identified.
